Chapter 11: The Name That Wouldn't Stay

spans.text: Captain Cubemelon counted to six and stopped at six.

He did it the way some people hum, the numbers arriving on their own behind the blue lens, soft and orderly, one badge at a time. Green Hills, lit. Sand Canyon, lit. Frost Cave, the blue cave glowing steady. Sky Islands, pale and bright. Mech Workshop, the silver gear turning slow. And the loop home, the route that meant you could always come back. Six little suns in a ring around the tall face of the Master Gate, burning where he had left them, and the counting of them was a small private gift he kept finding again, the way you find a coin in a coat you have not worn since spring.

He did not count the seventh slot. There was nothing there to count, only the pale smooth center of the ring where no badge had ever sat, and a leader who counts an empty thing has already started reaching for it. So he counted to six and stopped at six, and the stopping was its own quiet work.

The air near the gate tasted faintly of static, a thin metal tang on the back of the tongue, the way it always did. Off to his left the locked arch hummed its low forever-hum, dark and shut, the half-cube-and-a-line carved cool into its keystone. He kept his back to it. That was the muscle nobody had ever taught him he had, the not-looking, the not-turning-the-page, the daily work of leaving a thing alone.
There was a different number, the one he never said out loud.
Four.

Four flickers still loose on the map, out where the worlds gave way to static. Drip's ledger marked them at four scattered corners of the dark, four faint sparks of unfinished green, and for a whole long season home they had sat far apart and far off, the way the last few lights go out in a house settling down to sleep. You did not talk about a thing that stayed still and far away. Four was the number you left at the edge of the page.

But he knew where they were. That was the part of him he was quietest about. Even content, even with his face to the gold and his back to the trouble, some small reader behind the lens kept a finger on the last four flickers the way you keep a finger on a page so you do not lose your place. He had not turned to that page in days, and he was proud of it in a way he would never admit, because admitting it would mean admitting how hard the not-turning had been.

It was a strange muscle, the not-looking, and nobody had ever told him he had one. For years he had thought a good leader was the one who saw the trouble first and named it first and moved on it first, and the seeing had felt like duty and the not-seeing like cowardice. It had taken a whole long arc of getting it wrong to learn the harder shape of it: that there was a cost to chasing a thing, a quiet cost, paid not by him but by the people standing behind him when he bolted. Every flicker he had ever lunged at he had lunged at alone, and every time he lunged alone he stretched the team thin behind him like a rope pulled to its last fiber. So now he kept the four flickers in the corner of his attention and did not turn to them, and the not-turning was its own small daily work, the kind nobody watched and nobody praised, which was the only reason it had ever taught him anything.
He's doing the numbers,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip Pop said, to no one, fondly. She hung upside down off the low wall with her antenna curled and the little heart on her chest glowing soft morning pink.
You can always tell. He gets the face.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: It's his only face,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: said Ember Slice. She sat with the blue tool-sword across her knees, not sharpening it, only turning it so it threw one thin idle line of light back and forth across the grass. Tick. Tick. A beat so small no one was meant to step on it. She had learned to be still, and now she filled the stillness with a rhythm nobody had to mind.
Brick Bloom did not look up from her sketchpad. She was drawing the gate in patient brown lines, six lights and all, the kind of lines that made a thing look more like itself than a window would.
He has two faces,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick said.
The numbers face, and the face he makes right before he says slow.
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Patch Bolt laughed, the helpless bark he was always trying to swallow. He sat in a loose nest of his own tools with his hands folded on top of them, which was, for Patch, a small daily act of heroism. Nothing was broken. There was nothing to fix. He had learned that hands folded over good tools were better than hands reaching for a thing that was not broken yet, and so he sat on his fingers and laughed instead.
Thirteen home,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: said Drip Byte, from the wall, the cyan ledger glowing up off his tablet. It was thick now, thicker than it had ever been. Thirteen entries, each one a small block that had once flickered nonsense and now sat readable, logged, labeled, kept. Not deleted. Never deleted. Drip had built his whole self around that one rule. He scrolled the column slowly, the way some people pet a sleeping animal.
Thirteen safe,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: he said again, because counting them was a thing he liked.
Mm,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: said the Captain, who was listening to all of it while he counted. Six routes. Thirteen blocks. The two best numbers he knew.

Thirteen logged, the ledger said, and four flickering. That was the real count of the world this morning, and only the Captain and Drip carried both halves of it without flinching. Thirteen they had kept, one cold square at a time, across a season of careful mornings: thirteen frightened scribbles read and labeled and tucked warm into the cyan column, every one a friend they had decided to keep instead of erase. And four still loose. He let himself not say the four. He had gotten good at not saying the four. It was one more shape of the same muscle, the leaving-a-thing-at-the-edge-of-the-page, and he had practiced it so long that it almost passed, most mornings, for peace.

It was the kind of morning nobody knew what to do with, no trouble in it, no fall, no bright brave thing to point at. Just seven people in the gold, each holding the small piece of the day that was theirs, none of them holding it alone. Pip held the laughter. Ember held the beat. Brick held the meaning of six. Drip held the record. And the Captain held the count, and the count held them all, and the holding was so quiet and so complete that for one more breath nobody felt the fourth number leaning in from the cold edge of everything.
Then the Captain looked at the four flickers.
His lens drifted out on its own, past the six lit badges, past the warm ring of safe, out to the far cold edge of the map where the four faint sparks had sat scattered and quiet for so long.
And they were not scattered anymore.
He did not say anything. That was the first thing.

A younger Captain, the one who chased every flicker the instant it twitched, would already be three steps toward the edge of the park, wrench out, counting fast. This Captain stood still in the gold and made himself look slowly, made the numbers behind the lens slow down to match.
One. Out past Frost Cave's edge. It had drifted in.
Two. It had been at the far north corner for a whole season. It was not at the far north corner now. It had come down, and in, and to the left, toward.
Three. Toward the third one, which had moved to meet it.
Four.

The four faint flickers, which had sat at four lonely corners of the dark for as long as the team had been home, the four flickers nobody talked about because they never did anything, had pulled in close. Not scattered. Not still. Drawn together near the far gray reflection of the locked arch, into a loose trembling cluster, four lights leaning toward one shared center the way four cold things lean toward one small fire.

And they were braiding. That was the only word for it. The four faint greens had begun to thread between one another, in and out, slow, reaching, half a bridge trying to remember how to be a bridge, four lonely ends groping in the dark for a middle they had lost.

The Captain felt something he did not have a number for. It was not fear, exactly. It was the thing under fear, the thing you feel a beat before you understand why. Standing in the warm gold with six safe routes at his back, he looked at the four far flickers leaning into each other out in the cold, and before the leader in him could name a single mechanic, the person in him felt it first: that they had been very far apart, for a very long time, and that they were trying, finally, to get to one another, and that there was something in the trying that ached.
He did not know yet that one of them already knew his name.

He knew only that he could not look away, and that the not-looking-away had a familiar shape. The reach. The old leader's twitch toward a thing he had not decided to move toward yet. His hand had found the Gravity Wrench at his belt without his asking it to.
Slow, he told himself, first, the way he always did. Slow.
You're not looking at the gold,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: said Moss Guard.

The Captain did not startle. You did not startle when Moss arrived. Moss arrived the way a wall arrives, which is to say he had been there for some time and you simply had not finished noticing. He stood a half-step off the Captain's right side, big and green and quiet, the moss soft on his stone shoulders, the shield resting low with its circular mark glowing a calm steady blue. He was not looking at the four flickers. He was looking at the Captain looking at them.

That was Moss's whole job, and always had been. Not to watch the trouble. To watch the people he loved decide what to do about the trouble, and to stand where he could catch them if they decided wrong.

For a whole season he had stood half-angled toward the locked arch, ready, because for a whole season the trouble had been that, the way the arch pulled at the Captain, the way it made him reach for a door instead of for his friends. Lately Moss had let that angle go. The Captain had stopped reaching, and Moss had eased one degree, like a held thing set gently down. Now the Captain's lens was out at the far edge of the map, and there was something in the set of his shoulders that Moss knew the shape of from a long way off. The reach, pointed somewhere new.
The Captain heard the unasked question in it. Are you reaching again.
I wasn't going to open it,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said, quietly. The arch hummed at his back, dark and shut. He had not been looking at the arch. But Moss's worry and the arch lived in the same place in him, and he answered the place.
I wasn't. I'm just.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: The lens stayed fixed on the four braiding lights.
Look.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Moss did not look where the Captain looked. Moss kept looking at the Captain.
I know,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: Moss said.

Two words. They held more than two words ever should. I know you weren't. I know you're better. I know whatever is pulling at you now, it is not the arch. The Captain's lens warmed one shade, the way it did when Moss said a small true thing, and for a breath the two of them stood in the gold, the leader and the wall, the way they had stood at the foot of a hundred routes.
Then the Captain made himself say the rest of it, because not saying it would have been a kind of reaching too.
The flickers moved,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: he said.
All four. They've come together, out at the edge. They're making something.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: He felt Moss's stillness change. Not break, just change, the way a guard shifts his weight onto the watchful foot. Moss looked, finally, where the Captain was looking, out at the four faint greens braiding slow in the cold, trying to be a bridge.
Far,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: Moss said.
Far,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain agreed.

But it was the kind of far that was getting less far, and they both knew it. You did not have to be a tech reader to read four lonely lights deciding, after a whole season of staying apart, to lean in close and reach for a middle. You did not have to measure anything to read, in the slow brave shy way they were doing it, that they were not reaching toward each other for nothing.
They were reaching the way you reach when you have finally, finally heard someone calling.

Something in that snagged at the Captain, low and unplaceable, and he set it aside before it could become a thought. Somewhere at the very start of all of it, on the first cold night any of them could remember, a block had flickered seven broken letters at him in the dark and the team had read it as a label, this belongs to the green one, and Drip had never logged it, only written, underneath, in a small unsure hand, do not delete. The Captain had not thought about that night in a long while. He did not think about it now, not all the way. But the snag stayed, the way a name you cannot place stays, and he kept a finger on it the way he kept a finger on the four, and turned, for the moment, to Moss.
Drip,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said, not turning around. His voice was the calm formal one, a shade more careful than usual, which was how you could always tell.
When you've finished counting the thirteen we kept.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Mm?
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip looked up.
Count the four we haven't,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said.
And then come tell me they're standing still.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Drip's antenna gave a single small twitch. He looked at the Captain's back, then out past the six lit badges to the far cold edge of the map, and his thumbs went quiet on the tablet, because the four faint flickers his ledger had marked at four scattered corners for a whole safe season were not at four scattered corners anymore.
They had come together. And the gap between them and here was, by the smallest readable amount, no longer as wide as it had been at dawn.
Huh,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said.
It was the smallest word. It carried a great deal.

Pip had gone quiet too. She had drifted upright without anyone noticing, the laughter folded away, the heart on her chest dimmed to a careful listening pink. She tilted her head at the far edge the way she tilted it at a sad pad or a quiet crack, the instinct that heard the weather in a room before the rest of them felt the cold.
It's not coming at us,
she said softly.
Everybody hear me. It's not pushing.
She watched the slow braid of the four greens, the shy reaching of them.
It's leaning. There's a difference.

The Captain knew the difference. He had spent a whole arc learning that there was one. A thing that pushed, you stood against. A thing that leaned, you had to decide what to do with, and deciding was harder than standing, and far harder than reaching, because reaching answered the question before you had asked it.

He looked at the four far flickers, and the want stirred in him quiet and old. Somewhere out past the place where the worlds gave out, four scattered things had spent a season finding each other, and a part of him, the part that had named the whole first long arc of him, wanted to go to them now, first, alone, before they could drift, before the trouble could finish arriving. The leader chases every flicker. That had been the shape of him once, every morning, for years.

The trouble with the want was that it never arrived looking like a want. It arrived looking like care. It said, very reasonably, in a voice he trusted because it was his own, that he was the one who could read the far thing, that he should spare the others the cold and the not-knowing, that a leader who let his friends stand in front of a riddle he could solve himself was not a leader at all. Every word of it was nearly true, and the nearly was the dangerous part. He had learned, slowly, to listen for the place where the care turned and pointed back at him, at the oldest small wish under all of it, the wish to be the one who reached the answer first and laid the solved thing down at his friends' feet like a gift. He could not always find the turn. Some mornings the care and the wanting lived so close together he could not tell which one was speaking.
He kept his hand on the wrench and he made the hand ease, and he did not move.
Not yet. Not first. Not alone.

Far out at the edge of the dark, the four little lonely blocks found one more thread of the bridge between them, and held it, and trembled, and did not let go: four scared small things who had each spent a whole season believing they were the only one left, learning, very slowly, that they were not. And the braided thing they were building leaned, ever so slightly, toward the warm gold ring of the Master Gate, toward the pale seventh slot and the locked arch and the team, the way a frightened thing leans toward the only light it has ever seen, hoping, this time, that the light will not look away.
The four little blocks were not trying to be a bridge.

They were trying to find each other. Out past the lip of Portal Park, where the violet-gold thinned into the gray static everyone had learned to call the between, the four flickers drifted toward one center the way cold hands drift toward one small fire. They did not know they were the last four. They did not know thirteen of their kind had already been read and labeled and tucked warm into a teal person's ledger like names in a book. They knew only the long ache of a route with no anchor, the job of holding a path open with nobody on the other end, and they knew, dimly, that holding was easier together than alone.

So they braided. Edge to edge, crack to crack, the way you lean four tired shoulders into one wall. A hexagon steadied. Then another. A half-rendered portal-mouth opened between them and breathed. It was not a trap. It was not a wall. It was four frightened things building the only thing they knew how to build, hoping that if they built it well enough, someone would finally come.
Nobody had, yet.
But somebody was coming now.
Six routes stable,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said, the way he said it every morning.
Six badges lit. One pale slot. One arch, closed.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: You don't have to count it,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said, bouncing along beside him on her staff.
It's the same every day. That's the whole point of it being good.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: I count it because counting it is how I hear that it didn't change,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said.
Pip considered this, upside down, her antenna trailing in the grass.
That is the saddest reassuring thing I have ever heard. I love it. Keep it.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: He almost smiled. He was getting better at almost-smiling. A season ago he would have walked this scout the way he walked everything, first and fast, the lens already open and reaching, measuring the trouble before the trouble had finished arriving. This morning he walked it in the middle of his team, a place he had had to teach himself to stand.

The middle was harder than the front. Nobody warned you about that. At the front you only had to be brave, you faced the dark and the rest of them faced your back, and bravery turned out to be the easy part. In the middle you had to wait. You had to feel the pull of the unread thing ahead and not answer it, had to let Drip's tablet reach for it instead of your own lens, let Pip's quiet listen for it instead of your own count, and trust that seven slow readings braided together would arrive somewhere truer than one fast one ever could. It went against every wire in him. He kept doing it anyway. That, he was beginning to understand, was the whole of the job now: not to be first to the answer, but to keep himself in the middle of the people who would find it with him.

Drip was a little ahead, the way Drip always was, tablet up, antenna tipped toward the gray. Moss kept a little behind, between the team and whatever came after them. Ember tapped a soft idle beat against her thigh with two fingers, not nervous, just keeping time the way some people breathe. Patch had his hands in his belt and not on a tool. Brick held her sketchpad open to a clean page, waiting to see what was worth drawing. The team had a shape now, and the shape was good, and the Captain walked inside it toward the edge of the world.
They had come to look at the flickers.
Last four,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said, not turning around.
I had them at four separate points yesterday at dusk. Drifting slow. Nothing alarming.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: He frowned at the screen.
They are no longer at four separate points.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Where are they,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said.
That's the thing.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip stopped walking.
They're at one.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: They came up over the last low rise of solid ground, where the grass gave out and the paving stones went broken and then went to nothing, and the between opened in front of them. The team stopped all together, without anyone saying stop, which was its own kind of answer.
The bridge had not been there yesterday.

It hung in the gray static a stone's throw out, a span of floating hexagons strung on nothing, each one half-rendered and humming, edges that could not decide whether to be solid. Between the hexes, faint portal-mouths opened and closed like something breathing in its sleep. Green cracks ran the length of it, soft and slow, spelling half-letters that dissolved before they finished. It was not ugly. That was the strange part. It was almost beautiful, the way frost on a window is beautiful, a fragile accidental thing that would not last the morning.

The Captain made himself look at all of it before he let himself want any of it. The way the light moved through the half-built tiles, gold pooling in some and draining out of others, so the whole span seemed to breathe in and breathe out. The way the cracks spelled and unspelled, patient and tireless, like a voice that had forgotten it was speaking and knew only that it must not stop. The way the edges trembled, not the tremble of a thing about to break, he understood slowly, but the tremble of a thing holding very hard against breaking, a thing clenched, the way a hand clenches when it has gripped something heavy far too long. It was the most fragile route he had ever seen. It was also, somehow, the most stubborn.
And it hung close.

Not out at the far gray edge where the trouble usually started. Close. Close to the broken stones. Close to home. The Captain turned his head, slow, and behind them across the park stood the Master Gate, six lit badges in their ring, the pale seventh slot at the center. The bridge in the static hung nearly in a line with that empty slot, as if the two of them were looking at each other.
Nothing had ever come this close to the seventh slot before.
Huh,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: said Patch, very quietly, in the exact tone the team had learned to listen for.
Pip was not joking now. She had gone still on her staff, her heart-glow dimmed to a careful pink, her head tilted the way it tilted when she was listening to something nobody else could hear yet.
It's not pushing at us,
she said softly.
Everybody feel that. It's not coming at us.
She paused.
It's more like it built a porch.
A porch,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: Ember said.
A porch is for company,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said.
You build one so somebody can come.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: A shape drifted up out of the gray at the bridge's mouth.

She came the way she always came, not walking, not flying, simply more there than she had been a moment before, a quiet violet figure with the soft outline of a portal where a face might be, drifting at the threshold of the thing the flickers had built. Portia Portal. The team eased a half-step toward her without thinking, the way you ease toward a friend in a strange room.
Portia,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said.
You've seen it form.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: I have watched it all night,
spans.speaker: Portia

spans.text: said Portia, in her patient drifting way.
It is very tired. It has worked very hard.
spans.speaker: Portia

spans.text: It's blocking the way to the slot,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain said, measuring already, the line of it, the gap, the angles.
If it's grown across the route between us and the seventh badge.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: It isn't blocking the way,
spans.speaker: Portia

spans.text: Portia said, before he could finish.
She turned, slow, toward the humming span.
It is the way.

The Captain opened his mouth, closed it. The sentence sat in the cold air and refused to resolve into something he could measure. It is the way. A bridge that was the route, not a thing across the route. The old itch started up behind his lens, the itch that said I do not understand this yet, so understand it, now, fast, before it moves.
That's not an answer,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: he said, more sharply than he meant to.
No,
spans.speaker: Portia

spans.text: Portia agreed, kindly.
It is half of one. You will have the rest when you have walked it.
spans.speaker: Portia

spans.text: She drifted back toward the static.
But not yet. It will not hold half a team. It barely holds itself.
spans.speaker: Portia

spans.text: Drip was already crouched at the broken edge, tablet flat in both hands, fanning cyan light across the gap toward the bridge. This was the part he was best at, the kneeling-down, the close-looking, the asking the tablet. He had read thirteen blocks with it. He pointed it at the span and asked the only question that mattered. What is this route.

The tablet thought. The fans of light reached the first hexagon, touched it, flinched. The screen filled with garbage. Not an error. Drip knew errors, errors were clean, a tidy box and a thing you could fix. This was worse. The screen tried to draw the bridge and could not decide what it was drawing, a label half-eaten, a save in the wrong order, a loop with no end, a path split three ways at once, every kind of broken he had ever logged, layered and flickering and refusing to be one thing.
The tablet made a sound it had never made before, a long low VVVV, and the cyan light stuttered.
Drip sat back on his heels. His antenna had gone very still.
I can't map it,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: he said, the way you admit something to a doctor.
Captain. I have read everything in this park. Thirteen blocks. Six worlds. I can't map this.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: He looked up, and for once the confidence number was simply gone, and what lay under it was honest and a little scared.

It's made of the four things I was never able to log. Label, save, loop, split, all four, all at once, braided. The tablet has nothing to compare it to because the tablet has never finished reading any of them.
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: And there it was. The Captain felt it stand up inside him, whole and familiar, the oldest thing he owned.
Then I'll find out.

The bridge would carry a single traveler anywhere they wanted to go. That was the whole of its trouble. Step onto it alone to solve it first, and it firmed up under your boot and welcomed you and held, and then behind you the way home un-rendered, the colors draining toward static, the voices of your friends thinning until they came apart in the air, the route you had walked unmaking itself one square at a time. It held for one, if that one was willing to be alone forever. It did not want a hero. It wanted a hand. And the badge was no nearer for any of it, because the badge had never been a thing one cube could reach by being first.

He did not know that yet. He could not know it yet, because nobody had walked it. He only felt the pull of it, the unread span hanging a stone's throw from the empty slot the whole long season had been walking toward, and every instinct he had pulled toward it at once. Scan it. Measure it. Step out onto the first hex, alone, lens open, and solve it, fast, before it could drift, before anyone else had to stand in the cold not understanding it. He was the leader. The unread route was the leader's to read.
His lens flicked open and reached for the span.

It came back with nothing. Worse than nothing, it came back with garbage, the same stutter the tablet had hit, the bridge refusing his measurement the way it had refused Drip's. He scanned it again, faster. Garbage again. A third time, faster still, and the cyan scan-line of his own lens-mark broke apart in the static and scattered, FZZZT, and for half a breath the Captain, who measured the world to feel safe in it, could not measure the thing closest to home, and the not-knowing closed like a hand around his chest.

So he did what he always did when he was scared. He got more precise. He took one step toward the broken edge, lens narrowing, jaw set, already planning the exact angle he would test the first hex from, the exact number of seconds he would let it hold his weight. He never finished the thought.
Slow.

One word, behind him, low and even. Moss had not moved much. He never moved much. But the big green figure had shifted his weight a quarter-turn, shield easing off his shoulder, and he watched the Captain the way he had watched him for a whole season once, watching him reach for a door instead of for his friends.
The Captain stopped with his boot on the last solid stone.
I'm being slow,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: he said.

He heard it. He heard exactly how it sounded, clipped and certain and too certain, the voice of someone who has decided a thing and reports it as fact. Slow was supposed to be a speed. He had turned it into a claim. He had said I am being slow the way Drip's tablet had once said route correct, confidently, and not quite truthfully, about a thing he had not actually checked.
He looked down at his own boot, one square from the edge of everything.
He was not being slow. He was being first. He had just dressed it up in careful clothes.

Moss did not say I know. He did not say you almost stepped. He did not say any of the long sentences. He shifted his weight back, just slightly, and let the shield settle against his shoulder, not a wall in front of the Captain, just a presence beside him, a known thing in a place with no known things.
Stand here,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: Moss said.
With us.
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: The Captain stood there. With them. It cost him something. The bridge hummed its fragile hum, close, unread, the slot pale behind it, the answer hanging right there in the static, and he made himself take his boot off the last stone and set it down on solid ground beside Drip's knee, beside Pip's staff, in the middle of the shape his team made. He put the wrench back through his belt without remembering reaching for it. His hand was a little unsteady. He hid that, the way he hid most things.
Okay,
he said, to all of them, and his voice came out level, which he was glad of.
We don't step on it. Not today. Not until we can read it.
He looked at Drip.
Log what you can. Even the garbage. Especially the garbage.
Don't delete it,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip said, half a smile. The oldest rule he had.
Don't delete it,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: the Captain agreed.

Brick had been drawing the whole time, quick sure lines, the bridge caught on the clean page with all its trembling edges. She held the pad up so they could see. She had drawn it not as a barrier across a gap but as a span reaching, one frayed end toward the broken stones, one toward the gray.
It's not pointed away from us,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick said, in her plain way, the way she named meanings out loud so they could not be eaten.
Whatever it is. It's pointed at us. I want everyone to remember that we all saw that.
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: We saw it,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: said Ember.
We saw it,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: said Pip, soft.
We saw it,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: said Patch, and Moss said nothing, which on Moss meant the same.

Drip thumbed the words into the ledger before they could fade, bridge points toward us, witnessed by all, and the date, and a small note he did not read aloud: do not delete. He had learned across a great many cold mornings that the moment to write a true thing down was the moment everyone agreed on it out loud, because agreement was the one thing the glitches could never chew. He logged it, and kept his eyes, for once, on the team instead of the screen.

The Captain looked at the drawing, and at the real thing humming behind it, and felt the itch in his lens go quiet, one degree, the way it had the night he had sat with his back to the arch and let a door wait.

They turned for home, and it was Pip who looked back. Pip always looked back, the same instinct that made her tilt her head at a sad pad or a quiet crack. She looked at the fragile bridge hanging in the gray, four tired flickers leaning into each other, holding up a porch for company that had not come.
And the bridge moved.

Not toward the slot. Not toward the arch. It drifted, slow, a hand's-breadth, toward the broken stones, toward the place where the team had just been standing. It settled there, hexes steadying a fraction, green cracks pulsing one soft TIK-KRR, and went still, as if it had inched as far as it dared and now waited, patient as a wrong answer, for the ones who had come to look.
Captain,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said.
He turned.

It had come closer. While their backs were turned, the unreadable thing had given up a hand's-breadth of the safe gray distance and crept toward home, toward them, the way a frightened thing that wants to be found will follow at a distance and stop the instant you look at it. Nobody had been hurt. The bridge had not been attacking anyone. It was not coming for them with anything but the long shy patience of a thing that had built a porch and waited at a door. It had only leaned, one hand's-breadth, into the cold, and stopped.
It's not chasing us,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said quietly, and her heart-glow steadied, warm and certain.
Everybody hear me. It's not chasing. It came to find us. It built a porch and nobody came, so it walked to the door.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: The Captain looked at the bridge that had not been there yesterday, close now, closer than anything had ever come to the seventh slot, leaning toward his team in the gray like something that had held a path open alone for a very long time and had finally, finally heard footsteps. He did not reach for it. He stood in the middle of his friends, on solid ground, and made himself only look.
Then we'll come back,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: he said.
Together. When we can read it.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: The bridge settled a shade closer, as if it had come to find them, and the want in him said go first and the new muscle said not yet. Behind him, far across the brightening park, the locked arch hummed its faint patient hum, and its old cut symbol caught the gold for half a heartbeat and held it, a beat longer, maybe, than it ever had before.
The Captain did not see that. He would see it later.
